records.sourceFile: Recovery of the autonomic nervous system following football training among Division I collegiate football athletes - The influence of intensity and time.pdf

paper.citation: Wittels SH, Renaghan E, Wishon MJ, Wittels HL, Chong S, Wittels ED, et al. Recovery of the Autonomic Nervous System Following Football Training Among Division I Collegiate Football Athletes: The Influence of Intensity and Time. Heliyon. 2023;9(7):e18125.
paper.abstract: This prospective observational study examined how the duration and intensity of football training related to autonomic recovery and function 24 hours later in male Division I athletes.
paper.tldr: More time at the highest heart-rate thresholds was associated with poorer next-day cardiac recovery in one college football team. Use the signal to support individualized planning, not as a universal cutoff or causal rule.
paper.methods: Fifty male Division I football athletes wore ECG-capable armband monitors during 128 training sessions over 135 days of a 25-week season, yielding 2,735 observations. Regression models related time within heart-rate thresholds to next-day resting heart rate and heart-rate recovery.
paper.findings: Longer duration at 150 and 160 bpm thresholds showed stronger associations with higher next-day resting heart rate and slower heart-rate recovery than lower-intensity exposure. The authors interpreted the highest-intensity bouts as requiring more than 24 hours for autonomic restoration.
paper.limitations: The study assessed only the 24-hour time point, included one male football program, and did not control sleep, nutrition, hydration, or recovery treatment. Observational associations cannot establish an individual causal threshold, and several authors had financial relationships with the device company.
paper.practicalImplications: Track high-intensity duration alongside the athlete's next-day response and broader workload. When recovery markers and context agree, shorten strenuous bouts, extend between-session recovery, or modify the next exposure, then verify the response.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that recovery needs depend on intensity, duration, sleep, fueling, hydration, and accumulated work. Encourage honest reporting rather than presenting a device threshold as a pass-fail grade.
paper.rtp: During reconditioning, use cardiac response only as an adjunct to symptoms, tissue status, strength, movement, conditioning, and graded football exposure. One heart-rate pattern does not determine readiness.

records.sourceFile: Recreational and ergogenic substance use and substance use disorders in elite athletes- a narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: McDuff D, Stull T, Castaldelli-Maia JM, Hitchcock ME, Hainline B, Reardon CL. Recreational and Ergogenic Substance Use and Substance Use Disorders in Elite Athletes: A Narrative Review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(12):754-760.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarized prevalence, patterns, risk factors, performance effects, and interventions for recreational and performance-enhancing substance use among elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Substance patterns vary substantially by sport and population, and diagnosed disorder prevalence in elite athletes was unknown. Build confidential support and referral systems without stereotyping or diagnosing from one behavior.
paper.methods: The authors conducted a broad literature search for studies comparing athlete and non-athlete substance use or describing demographic, sport, risk, motive, performance, and intervention patterns across major recreational and performance-enhancing substance classes.
paper.findings: Alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, prescribed opioids, and stimulants were commonly reported and often lower than in non-athletes, while binge alcohol, oral tobacco, non-prescription opioids, and anabolic-androgenic steroid use were higher in some athlete groups, particularly power and collision sports. Use varied by country, sport, sex, ethnicity, and competitive level.
paper.limitations: No included evidence established the prevalence of diagnosed substance-use disorders in elite male or female athletes, and few studies used direct comparison groups. Definitions, self-report, testing, populations, and substances were heterogeneous, and a narrative review cannot provide pooled certainty.
paper.practicalImplications: Create confidential education, screening, clinical assessment, and referral pathways that distinguish occasional use, misuse, and disorder. Review pain, sleep, stress, mental health, medication, supplements, team culture, and current antidoping rules together.
paper.athleteDev: Use nonjudgmental conversations that protect trust and make help-seeking safe. Explain performance, health, legal, and antidoping risks while avoiding assumptions based on sport, position, or identity.
paper.rtp: Substance use can interact with symptoms, medication, sleep, judgment, hydration, and adherence. Return decisions require clinical assessment and a support plan when use creates safety or functional concerns.

records.sourceFile: Protect the player, protect the game - Reflections from ex-professional rugby union players on law changes, protective equipment, and duty of care in the professional game.pdf

paper.citation: Daly E, Blackett AD, Pearce AJ, Ryan L. Protect the Player, Protect the Game: Reflections from Ex-Professional Rugby Union Players on Law Changes, Protective Equipment, and Duty of Care in the Professional Game. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2022;7(4):91.
paper.abstract: This qualitative study interviewed retired professional male rugby-union players about concussion management, protective equipment, law changes, workload, return to play, and duty of care.
paper.tldr: Former players described pressure and test manipulation and wanted medically independent, more conservative return decisions. Their accounts support stronger safeguards but do not estimate how common these practices are today.
paper.methods: Twenty-three retired professional male rugby-union players, 61% with international test experience, completed interviews that were analyzed for themes concerning duty of care, concussion return to play, protective equipment, and law or workload changes.
paper.findings: Participants reported pressure from coaches or clubs to play with symptoms and described manipulating concussion tests. They favored independent medical decisions, longer return processes, ongoing care after retirement, and reduced match or contact-training exposure; they did not believe current protective equipment or law changes eliminated concussion risk.
paper.limitations: The small retrospective male sample retired within the prior decade and may be affected by selection, recall, and social-desirability bias. Policies, laws, workloads, and clinical practice may have changed, and qualitative reports are not prevalence estimates.
paper.practicalImplications: Separate medical clearance authority from performance pressure, protect symptom disclosure, prohibit coaching influence over testing, audit return-to-play processes, and manage contact volume. Extend referral and follow-up support beyond roster status when feasible.
paper.athleteDev: Make clear that symptom reporting protects the athlete and teammates and will not be treated as a character failure. Teach why trying to beat a concussion test can increase long-term risk.
paper.rtp: Concussion return should remain clinician-led, symptom-responsive, and progressively exposed to cognitive, physical, and contact demands. Equipment use never replaces recognition, removal, assessment, and conservative progression.

records.sourceFile: Relative training load and match outcome - Are professional soccer players actually undertrained during the in-season.pdf

paper.citation: Modric T, Jelicic M, Sekulic D. Relative Training Load and Match Outcome: Are Professional Soccer Players Actually Undertrained During the In-Season? Sports. 2021;9(10):139.
paper.abstract: This observational study examined associations between training-to-match running-load ratios within the weekly microcycle and subsequent match outcome in professional soccer.
paper.tldr: One team won more often after a week with high-intensity work in midweek, greater earlier volume, and lower final-two-day volume. The pattern is a periodization hypothesis, not proof that manipulating a ratio causes wins.
paper.methods: Twenty-one professional players were monitored by GPS during 67 training sessions and 14 official matches. Training-to-match ratios were calculated by day for total, low-, running-, and high-intensity distance plus acceleration and deceleration variables, then correlated with win, draw, or loss.
paper.findings: Better match outcome correlated with more high-intensity-running load three days before the match, more total and low-intensity distance and acceleration-deceleration volume five days before it, and lower volume in those variables one and two days before the match.
paper.limitations: Only one team and 14 matches were observed, and eligible players completed full training and the following match. Correlation cannot isolate effects from opponent, tactics, selection, schedule, score state, or other confounding, and internal load was unavailable.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider early-week volume, a purposeful midweek high-speed exposure, and reduced final-two-day volume, but calibrate the pattern to the athlete and schedule. Evaluate it locally with readiness, availability, and performance rather than match result alone.
paper.athleteDev: Explain how the week builds, exposes, and tapers different qualities so athletes understand why hard and easy days are sequenced. Use feedback to individualize without promising that one loading pattern determines outcome.
paper.rtp: Returning players should not inherit the team ratio automatically. Progress their high-speed, acceleration, deceleration, and soccer volume from individual capacity toward role-specific training and match demands.

records.sourceFile: Residual deficits in reactive strength indicate incomplete restoration of athletic qualities following ACL reconstruction in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Read PJ, Davies WT, Bishop C, McAuliffe S, Wilson MG, Turner AN. Residual Deficits in Reactive Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players. Journal of Athletic Training. 2023;58(5):423-429.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study evaluated a repeated single-leg vertical hop as a measure of residual function after ACL reconstruction in soccer players completing rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: Soccer players completing ACL rehabilitation still showed lower repeated-hop performance and greater asymmetry than controls. Vertical rebound testing adds sensitivity but cannot clear an athlete by itself.
paper.methods: Seventy-three soccer players with ACL reconstruction and 195 matched controls completed a 10-second single-leg vertical hop measuring jump height, reactive-strength index, and asymmetry. Drop-jump performance, isokinetic knee-extension torque, and self-reported knee function were examined as predictors.
paper.findings: Between-limb differences were present only in the ACLR group, whose asymmetry exceeded controls. Single-leg drop-jump reactive strength and knee-extension torque predicted portions of repeated-hop height and reactive-strength performance, suggesting residual strength and stretch-shortening-cycle deficits.
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional comparisons lacked preinjury baselines and cannot show prospective reinjury risk or successful return. Control matching does not define an individual's target, and the predictor models left substantial performance variance unexplained.
paper.practicalImplications: Include repeatable vertical rebound tasks when they add information beyond horizontal hop distance. Inspect height, contact time, reactive strength, asymmetry, symptoms, and strategy across serial tests rather than using a single score.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that completing rehabilitation or restoring horizontal distance may not fully restore rapid elastic function. Use test results to target quadriceps strength and reactive loading without framing asymmetry as failure.
paper.rtp: Combine vertical rebound testing with symptoms, knee examination, strength, power, movement quality, confidence, conditioning, change of direction, and progressive soccer exposure. No single limb-symmetry threshold is sufficient.

records.sourceFile: The distribution of match activities relative to the maximal intensities in elite soccer players - Implications for practice.pdf

paper.citation: Riboli A, Esposito F, Coratella G. The Distribution of Match Activities Relative to the Maximal Intensities in Elite Soccer Players: Implications for Practice. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022;30(5):463-474.
paper.abstract: This match-monitoring study characterized how average, above-average, and one-minute peak locomotor demands were distributed in elite Italian soccer.
paper.tldr: Whole-match averages substantially diluted short high-intensity demands, and positions differed in distance accumulated above average. Prescribe from multiple references because a match peak is still not an athlete's maximum capacity.
paper.methods: One hundred forty-eight Serie A players contributed 680 samples across 46 official matches. Total distance, high- and very-high-speed running, sprinting, acceleration, and deceleration were expressed relative to each player's one-minute match peak, with time and distance above the 90-minute average also calculated.
paper.findings: The 90-minute average was 59.6% of one-minute peak for total distance but only 26.2% for high-speed running, 16.0% for very-high-speed running, 9.3% for sprinting, 19.2% for acceleration, and 15.4% for deceleration. Distance above average differed by position.
paper.limitations: A match peak can remain below individual maximal capacity. Internal load, high-intensity action counts, directional change, venue, opponent, congestion, and seasonal timing were not included, and locomotor data do not capture all technical or tactical demand.
paper.practicalImplications: Build drills from a demand envelope that includes average, above-average duration, peak, position, and individual capacity. Combine soccer-specific play with supplemental running or neuromuscular work when drills do not reach the intended exposure.
paper.athleteDev: Show athletes why average match output is not the ceiling and why role-specific peak preparation matters. Pair external-load targets with perceived and physiological response.
paper.rtp: Progress from controlled individual intensity to position-specific peak and repeated-demand exposure, then team practice and competition. Match-derived targets must be scaled to current capacity and tissue tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Is additive manufacturing improving performance in sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Novak JI, Novak AR. Is Additive Manufacturing Improving Performance in Sports? A Systematic Review. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part P: Journal of Sports Engineering and Technology. 2021;235(3):163-175.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated empirical evidence for additively manufactured sporting equipment, protection, and comfort products across multiple sports.
paper.tldr: Some 3D-printed sports products performed better than conventional comparators, but most applications were isolated and weakly replicated. Validate fit, safety, durability, rules, and field performance before adoption.
paper.methods: Four databases were searched from 1984 through May 2019 under a PRISMA-based protocol. Twenty-six articles across 12 sports were analyzed for application, performance comparison, manufacturing process, software, scanning, and reported opportunities or constraints.
paper.findings: Ten articles reported improved product performance, eight similar performance, and five lower performance than conventional products. Running or walking dominated, half used powder-bed fusion, 42% used 3D scanning, and many failed to identify the printer or design software.
paper.limitations: The small, heterogeneous evidence base could not be pooled and was dominated by single studies. Sample size, laboratory transfer, long-term durability, material interfaces, postprocessing, regulation, and incomplete technical reporting constrain confidence and replication.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat additive manufacturing as a prototyping and customization pathway. Before athlete use, define the problem and comparator, verify material and fit, test safety and durability under representative load, confirm rules, and monitor failures and athlete response.
paper.athleteDev: Invite athlete input on fit and function without implying that customized or novel means superior. Record comfort, performance, skin or pressure issues, and durability over time.
paper.rtp: A customized brace, orthosis, guard, or equipment component needs clinical and engineering validation for the intended task. Do not let novelty accelerate exposure or replace established protection and capacity criteria.

records.sourceFile: Is melatonin as an ergogenic hormone a myth - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Drummond FR, Drummond LR, Campos HO, Fernandes JGRP, Monteiro MC, Lara HFG, et al. Is Melatonin as an Ergogenic Hormone a Myth? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Endocrine. 2024;83(2):302-321.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated melatonin supplementation for exercise performance and recovery and examined exercise-related melatonin secretion.
paper.tldr: Melatonin did not improve pooled aerobic or strength performance. Evidence for recovery was narrow and should not be generalized into a performance supplement recommendation.
paper.methods: Twenty-one studies met systematic-review criteria and 19 entered meta-analysis. Models examined time-trial and oxygen-uptake performance, strength, postexercise recovery biomarkers, and endogenous melatonin immediately and 60 minutes after exercise.
paper.findings: Supplementation did not improve time-trial, oxygen-uptake, or strength performance. Glutathione peroxidase increased, while other pooled recovery outcomes did not establish a broad ergogenic effect; exercise did not consistently change immediate or 60-minute melatonin secretion.
paper.limitations: Few studies were available, and some individuals contributed multiple outcomes or trials. Dose, timing, task, population, and recovery measures varied, and evidence for a general recovery benefit rested on limited biomarkers rather than consistent performance restoration.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use melatonin to enhance strength or endurance. If sleep or travel is the target, first address schedule, light, behavior, and sleep opportunity, then involve qualified medical or nutrition staff for product, dose, timing, interaction, and side-effect review.
paper.athleteDev: Separate sleep support from performance enhancement and discourage self-escalation. Ask athletes to report next-day drowsiness, unusual dreams, headaches, medication use, and product source.
paper.rtp: Melatonin is not a readiness marker or tissue-recovery treatment. Any use during rehabilitation should support an identified sleep plan and avoid side effects that impair training, driving, or clinical monitoring.

records.sourceFile: Is there rationale for the cuff pressures prescribed for blood flow restriction exercise - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Clarkson MJ, May AK, Warmington SA. Is There Rationale for the Cuff Pressures Prescribed for Blood Flow Restriction Exercise? A Systematic Review. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2020;30(8):1318-1336.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined how blood-flow-restriction studies selected individualized cuff pressure and whether the selected percentage of occlusion pressure was justified.
paper.tldr: Even individualized BFR studies used 30% to 100% occlusion pressure, rarely with clear rationale. Measure with the actual setup, screen risk, and avoid a universal pressure prescription.
paper.methods: Fifty-one acute or chronic BFR-exercise studies that measured limb or arterial occlusion pressure were identified and assessed with a bespoke 13-point quality tool. Pressure, population, cuff, exercise, methodology, and stated rationale were extracted.
paper.findings: Prescribed pressure ranged from 30% to 100% of measured occlusion pressure, and only seven study applications justified the selected percentage. Individualization addressed some equipment and participant variability but did not create consistent prescription or reporting.
paper.limitations: The review did not compare adaptation or adverse outcomes across pressures. Heterogeneity in population, exercise, cuff width and material, device regulation, body position, and reporting prevents identification of an ideal pressure.
paper.practicalImplications: Screen contraindications, measure occlusion in the exercise-specific body position with the actual cuff, prescribe the lowest justified individualized pressure, monitor symptoms and response, and document equipment and method for repeatability.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that more pressure is not automatically more effective. Athletes should immediately report numbness, unusual pain, discoloration, dizziness, or symptoms beyond expected exertion.
paper.rtp: BFR can supplement low-load rehabilitation when clinically appropriate, but it does not replace progressive tissue loading. Pressure and exercise must be individualized and supervised within the medical plan.

records.sourceFile: Isometric training and long -term   adaptations; effects of muscle length, intensity and intent- A systematic   review.pdf

paper.citation: Oranchuk DJ, Storey AG, Nelson AR, Cronin JB. Isometric Training and Long-Term Adaptations: Effects of Muscle Length, Intensity, and Intent: A Systematic Review. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;29(4):484-503.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined how muscle length, contraction intensity, and intent influence medium- to long-term morphological, neural, tendon, and performance adaptations to isometric training.
paper.tldr: Longer muscle lengths favored hypertrophy and transfer, ballistic intent favored rapid force, and higher intensity appeared important for tendon adaptation. Prescribe to the target rather than using one generic isometric protocol.
paper.methods: Four databases were searched for human studies lasting at least three weeks. Twenty-three research outputs were quality-evaluated and synthesized by joint angle or muscle length, contraction intensity, intent, volume, and morphological, neural, tendon, or performance outcome.
paper.findings: Long-muscle-length training generally produced greater hypertrophy and dynamic transfer than shorter-length work. Ballistic intent improved activation and rapid force production, contractions at or above 70% MVC appeared necessary for tendon structure and function, and hypertrophy and maximal force improved across intensities.
paper.limitations: The number of direct comparisons was limited and interventions, muscle groups, doses, and outcomes varied. Closed-chain and dynamic transfer, fatigue, rehabilitation populations, contraction subtypes, free-weight use, and sequencing with later dynamic training need more research.
paper.practicalImplications: Start with the adaptation required: use tolerable longer-muscle-length positions for morphology and transfer, fast intent for early force, and sufficiently high force for tendon goals when clinically appropriate. Progress volume, angle, intensity, and intent separately.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that an isometric can target pain-tolerant loading, position-specific strength, tendon force, or rapid recruitment depending on execution. Quality and intent matter even when no movement is visible.
paper.rtp: Use isometrics to bridge capacity at controlled joint angles, then demonstrate transfer through dynamic, elastic, multidirectional, and sport-specific tasks. Isometric improvement alone does not establish return readiness.

records.sourceFile: Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling - A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Zhao Z, Liu Y, Xu K. Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling: A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2026;25:84-111.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis evaluated agility training that coupled perception with action in team-sport athletes and explored moderators and dose-response patterns.
paper.tldr: Perception-action training improved reactive agility, but the apparent seven-to-eight-week dose was not a proven optimum. Use representative stimuli and monitor total load while accounting for limited female and non-soccer evidence.
paper.methods: Twenty-eight studies met the review criteria, and 26 contributed 53 effect sizes after influential-study exclusions. Three-level models pooled reactive-agility, preplanned-agility, and reaction outcomes; subgroup and meta-regression analyses explored population and training dose.
paper.findings: Reactive-agility performance improved with a large effect (0.65), preplanned agility with a moderate effect (0.55), and reaction outcomes with a nonsignificant moderate estimate (0.52). Favorable effects clustered around seven to eight weeks, more than three weekly sessions, and 20 to 25 minutes per session.
paper.limitations: Certainty was moderate for reactive agility and low or very low for secondary outcomes. Heterogeneity, possible publication or outcome-reporting bias, soccer and basketball dominance, female underrepresentation, inconsistent training-load reporting, and sparse retention data limit dose claims.
paper.practicalImplications: Use decision-rich drills with representative visual or human stimuli and retain separate change-of-direction capacity work where needed. Progress complexity and exposure from athlete response rather than copying the pooled frequency as a formula.
paper.athleteDev: Develop scanning, anticipation, decision speed, and movement execution together. Give athletes feedback on the decision and solution, not only completion time.
paper.rtp: Reintroduce agility from predictable movement to increasingly representative perception-action tasks, then uncontrolled team play. Account for physical, cognitive, and total-session load throughout the progression.

records.sourceFile: Qualitative and quantitative situational characteristics of muscle strains in sports - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Finnern LS, Wilke J, Willwacher S, Pasanen K, Hollander K, Dalos D, et al. Qualitative and Quantitative Situational Characteristics of Muscle Strains in Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;60(3):211-226.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized video-recorded situational and kinematic characteristics of indirect and non-contact muscle injuries across sports and muscle groups.
paper.tldr: Most recorded strains were non-contact and many were running-related, but patterns differed by muscle and sport. Prepare athletes for representative high-force length changes without claiming one video position caused the injury.
paper.methods: Twenty-one video-analysis studies reported 728 indirect or non-contact muscle injuries. Contact mechanism, activity, movement direction, joint position, timing, and muscle-specific patterns were synthesized qualitatively and, when possible, quantitatively.
paper.findings: Seventy-four percent of injuries were non-contact and nearly half were running-related. Many occurred during active rapid muscle-tendon length change, with recurring but distinct patterns for hamstring, adductor, rectus-femoris, and calf injuries and additional sport-specific kicking, reaching, deceleration, or perturbation situations.
paper.limitations: Football and hamstring evidence dominated, female athletes and several muscles were underrepresented, terminology and methods varied, and study quality ranged from low to high. Video angle, quality, rater expertise, and missing clinical or imaging context limit causal inference.
paper.practicalImplications: Prepare the relevant muscle for its sport-specific high-force, long-length, sprinting, kicking, acceleration, deceleration, reaching, and perturbation demands. Confirm proposed prevention elements prospectively rather than assuming mechanism resemblance guarantees efficacy.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to build exposure to the situations the sport requires instead of fearing a single movement. Progress speed, range, force, fatigue, and uncertainty while maintaining technical options.
paper.rtp: Rehabilitation should recreate the injured muscle's likely demand profile and the athlete's position and sport situations. Video patterns can guide exposure selection but cannot replace clinical diagnosis, tissue criteria, confidence, or full practice progression.
